findings.title: Do not pipe unpinned remote script into sh in Dockerfile
findings.whyItBreaks: The new build step fetches https://example.com/install.sh and executes it as root inside the image via `| sh`, with no version pin, no source allowlist, and no checksum/signature verification. Every `docker build` runs whatever the remote endpoint serves at that moment, so a compromised DNS/registry/TLS path or a changed script silently injects arbitrary code into the image. Because curl lacks `-f`, HTTP error bodies (4xx/5xx) are also piped into the shell as if they were valid script, so a failed/error response can be executed rather than rejected.

findings.title: Pipeline masks curl download failure, so install errors are silent
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes under Alpine's default /bin/sh, which has no `pipefail`, so the RUN's exit status is `sh`'s status, not curl's. If the download fails (DNS/network/TLS error), curl emits nothing, `sh` reads empty stdin, exits 0, and the build succeeds as if the installer had run (previously_reached: Docker build failure). Even with curl succeeding, `-s` without `-f` treats an HTTP 4xx/5xx body as success and feeds the error page to the shell. Failure and success become indistinguishable to the build, so the image ships without the intended install and nothing flags it.

findings.title: Do not curl|sh unpinned remote script in Docker build
findings.whyItBreaks: This RUN executes whatever https://example.com/install.sh serves, with the build's privileges, and bakes the result into the image. There is no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and no digest pin on the fetched artifact, so the image is non-reproducible and every rebuild trusts an unauthenticated third-party endpoint; a compromised/changed response (or the placeholder example.com, a non-distribution host) is executed as shell. Compounding it, curl is invoked without -f and the pipe masks curl's exit code (Alpine /bin/sh has no pipefail), so a network failure or HTTP 4xx/5xx yields an empty or error-body script that sh runs and exits 0 — the build 'succeeds' while the intended install never happened, shipping a silently broken image.

findings.title: Do not curl-pipe an unverified remote script at image build time
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR adds `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh`, which downloads and executes arbitrary remote code during `docker build`. The artifact is unpinned (no version/commit), unverified (no checksum or signature), and fetched over a network at build time, so the build is non-reproducible and the image contents can be silently replaced by anyone who controls that endpoint or the TLS path. Because it is piped straight into `sh`, a truncated/failed download (e.g. network error, DNS failure) yields empty stdin that `sh` exits 0 on, so the failure is swallowed and the build continues with whatever partial state resulted. This is an injection surface executed as root in the image, not a style concern.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing, conflating absent key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing specifically so callers can tell 'key not present' apart from 'key present with value ""'. The new exported wrapper drops that error with `v, _ := Load(...)` and returns only the string. Because an empty string is a legal stored value in map[string]string, every caller is FORCED to treat a genuinely-present "" identically to an absent key. Any caller that persists, reports, or branches on this value (e.g. 'config unset → apply default' vs 'config explicitly set to empty') will silently misbehave on the absent case, since the failure signal never reaches it. The defect is the public contract itself and ships now regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing with empty
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault drops Load's error with `v, _ :=`, returning "" for a missing key. Load itself returns "" with a nil error when the key exists but maps to an empty string, so a caller of LoadOrDefault observes the exact same "" whether the key is absent or is present-and-empty. The failure signal (ErrMissing) is irreversible once discarded, and this is an exported package-level function, so the unusable contract ships now: every eventual caller is forced to treat "key not found" as real data (e.g. persisting/reporting ""). Additionally the name promises an "or default" value but the function takes no default parameter, so the implicit default is always the empty string.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing keys with empty values
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) for an absent key (src/store.go:10) but ("", nil) for a key that is present with an empty value (src/store.go:12). LoadOrDefault drops the error with `_`, so both cases return "". Callers cannot distinguish a missing key that should trigger a fallback/error from a genuine empty string, and acting on the fallback (defaulting, persisting, reporting) may silently treat absence as real data. As an exported symbol this is the shipped API contract even before any in-repo caller exists.

findings.title: Run returns before results are sent; ordering and completion lost
findings.whyItBreaks: Base body sent each result synchronously, so Run returned only after all N values were delivered in jobs order. The new body launches one goroutine per job and returns at once, so: (a) results arrive in nondeterministic order, (b) a caller that closes/reuses results immediately after Run returns can race a still-pending send and panic with 'send on closed channel' or silently drop values, and (c) with an unbuffered or slow consumer, each goroutine blocks on the send forever, leaking one goroutine per job. The three-line change reverses the function's observable contract for every caller.

findings.title: Run returns before sends complete; goroutine sends race close(results)
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change Run sent every result synchronously and only returned after all sends completed, so a caller could do `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` and then range over a fully-populated channel. Now Run spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately (line 7-9), while the `results <- j*2` sends happen later on unmanaged goroutines. Any caller that closes results on Run return hits a send-on-closed-channel panic, and any caller that drains a fixed expected count or relies on job order gets truncated or reordered results. Concurrency is also unbounded (one goroutine per element of jobs) instead of the previous steady one-at-a-time send. The ctx parameter is still unused, so there is no cancellation to stop the leaked goroutines if the consumer stops draining.

findings.title: Run returns before sends finish; results unordered and senders outlive the call
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code sent synchronously in slice order, so when Run returned every value had been delivered and `results` held `jobs[i]*2` in i order. The new body fires one goroutine per job and returns immediately: (1) delivery order is now scheduler-dependent, so any caller pairing the i-th received value with jobs[i] is wrong; (2) the sends happen-after Run returns, so a caller that follows the natural pattern `worker.Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` can panic with `send on closed channel`, and a consumer that stops reading (e.g. on ctx cancellation, since Run ignores ctx) leaves every spawned goroutine permanently blocked on the unbuffered send. ctx is accepted but never observed, so there is no cancellation path out of the leak.

findings.title: Widened delete check grants cross-tenant and non-admin deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate previously required BOTH session.isAdmin and matching tenantId. With `||`, a non-admin session now passes whenever session.tenantId === record.tenantId (privilege escalation within a tenant), and an admin session now passes for records in ANY tenant (cross-tenant deletion). Any caller using this as the authorization gate for delete will permit both bypasses.

findings.title: Authorization bypass: OR grants cross-tenant and non-admin record deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous guard required BOTH session.isAdmin AND session.tenantId === record.tenantId, so only a tenant's own admin could delete its records. With `||`, any admin (session.isAdmin=true) is allowed to delete records belonging to ANY tenant, and any non-admin whose tenantId matches the record is also allowed. This bypasses tenant isolation and privilege checks: canDeleteRecord({isAdmin:true,tenantId:'A'}, {tenantId:'B'}) and canDeleteRecord({isAdmin:false,tenantId:'A'}, {tenantId:'A'}) both now return true when they must return false.

findings.title: Restore per-tenant admin guard in canDeleteRecord (|| bypasses authz)
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate previously required `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId`. Changing to `||` grants two independent authorization bypasses on the delete path: (1) an admin of tenant A now passes for a record in tenant B (cross-tenant authority, previously blocked); (2) any non-admin user whose tenantId merely matches the record's tenantId now passes, so an ordinary user can delete records they do not own (ownerId is ignored entirely). Either branch admits deletes that were intended to be rejected, enabling unauthorized record deletion / data loss.

findings.title: catch-all in parseSettings silently discards validation errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, JSON.parse errors and the explicit `throw new Error("bad theme")`/`"bad fontSize"` validations propagated to the caller, so nothing was written. The new `catch { return { ...DEFAULTS }; }` maps every failure (malformed JSON, missing/wrong-typed theme, missing/wrong-typed fontSize) to a legitimate value, so a caller can no longer distinguish "parsed these settings" from "input was invalid". The single live caller, updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20), reads that fallback and unconditionally persists it at line 22: `updateFontSize("{bad json}", 18, save)` now calls `save('{"theme":"light","fontSize":18}')`, silently overwriting the stored theme with "light". Previously that call threw and the `save` callback never ran. Invalid-but-recoverable input (e.g. a valid theme with a bad fontSize) is also reset rather than surfaced.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows parse/validation errors and returns DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch-all maps every failure (invalid JSON, non-string theme, non-number fontSize) to `{...DEFAULTS}`, destroying the failure signal. The only caller, updateFontSize @src/settings.ts:20, then mutates that fabricated object and calls save(), so a partially-valid stored config is silently overwritten with defaults. Example: raw='{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"16"}' previously threw 'bad fontSize' at line 12 and updateFontSize never saved; now parseSettings returns {theme:'light',fontSize:14}, the user's 'dark' theme is discarded, and `{"theme":"light","fontSize":16}` is persisted. Callers can no longer distinguish 'parse failed' from 'successfully parsed defaults'.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows invalid-input errors and resets settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change parseSettings threw on JSON.parse failure and on the explicit 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' checks; callers could distinguish invalid input from valid settings. The new catch converts EVERY such failure into { ...DEFAULTS } with no log or signal. updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22) consumes parseSettings and immediately persists the result via save(JSON.stringify(settings)): when the stored raw is corrupt or has a wrong-typed field, the user's existing theme/settings are silently overwritten with light/14 instead of the write being aborted, destroying recoverable configuration and hiding the fault. Because parseSettings is exported, any external caller is also forced to conflate 'failed' with a legitimate default value.

findings.title: buildReport reports artifacts from a ref other than builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, artifacts were fetched with build.artifactsAt(commit) where commit = build.ref(branch), so the returned BuildReport paired `builtFrom: commit` with artifacts that belong to that same commit. The change adds `const verified = build.ref("verified")` and returns `artifacts: build.artifactsAt(verified)` while leaving `builtFrom: commit` untouched. Build.ref and Build.artifactsAt are independent lookups (interface at src/report.ts:1-4), so 'verified' and the branch ref need not resolve to the same commit. Whenever they differ, the report advertises builtFrom = branch commit but lists artifacts belonging to the 'verified' ref, producing an inconsistent/misattributed report with no error or signal that the two come from different commits.

findings.title: Report lists artifacts from hardcoded ref, not builtFrom commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` is set to `build.ref(branch)` (line 12) but `artifacts` is now fetched from `build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified"))` via a hardcoded "verified" ref (lines 13-14). For any branch whose commit is not identical to whatever the "verified" ref resolves to, the returned BuildReport claims artifacts were built from `commit` while actually listing artifacts from a different commit. The mismatch is silent — the report's own contract (builtFrom <-> artifacts) is violated and provenance consumers receive artifacts that do not belong to the reported commit. The previous code derived both fields from the same commit, so this is a behavior regression introduced by this diff.

findings.title: Report pairs branch commit with artifacts from hardcoded "verified" ref
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` is still resolved from the caller-supplied `branch` (line 12), but `artifacts` is now always fetched from `build.ref("verified")` instead of that same commit. Because `artifactAt` is keyed on the ref passed in, `buildReport(build, "main")` and `buildReport(build, "release")` now return identical artifact lists drawn from whatever `verified` points at, while `builtFrom` claims they came from the requested branch. Every caller therefore receives a report whose artifact set does not correspond to the commit it advertises, and the `branch` argument silently stops selecting artifacts for any non-"verified" ref. This is a behavior change on a public exported function with no in-repo compensating logic.

findings.title: Restore `limit` cap: recentEntries returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaced `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)` with `return sorted`, removing the only use of `limit` on the positive path. For any `limit > 0` the function now returns the entire reversed list instead of at most `limit` entries, contradicting its own contract ("Returns at most `limit` entries"). The sole caller `renderFeed(all)` calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and copies into a buffer sized for 20 (`new Array<string>(20)`) while looping `i < page.length`; since `page.length` can exceed 20, `out[i]` for i>=20 extends the array, so renderFeed emits every entry instead of capping at 20.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit and returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`, which capped the result. The new body reverses into `sorted`, special-cases only `limit <= 0`, then `return sorted` — the `slice(0, limit)` cap is gone. For any `limit > 0` the function now returns ALL entries (newest first) instead of at most `limit`, breaking the documented contract on line 1 and every caller that relies on the cap. The concrete live failure is `renderFeed` (src/feed.ts:9-12): it calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and copies `page[i]` into an array sized 20, but with more than 20 entries `page.length > 20` and the loop writes `out[20], out[21], …`, extending the array past 20 and returning an oversized feed.

The head body reverses into `sorted`, returns `[]` for limit<=0, but for limit>0 returns the full `sorted` array with no `.slice(0, limit)`. Substituting limit=20: recentEntries(['a'..'z'],20) now returns 26 reversed entries instead of 20, so renderFeed's fixed 20-slot page (new Array<string>(20) @src/feed.ts:10) is overrun — `out[i] = page[i]` for i>=20 grows the array, making the rendered feed unbounded in the number of source entries.

findings.title: Make entry-count match filtered rows
findings.whyItBreaks: This change makes `rows` contain only non-stale entries, but the `# entry-count` header at src/manifest.ts:22 still reports `entries.length`, which includes stale entries. Whenever any entry has `stale: true`, the manifest's declared count overstates the number of entries actually present, so any consumer that parses `# entry-count` as the number of data rows (or validates row count against it) mis-parses the manifest. Before this diff, count and rows agreed; the filter introduces the divergence.

findings.title: entry-count header no longer matches emitted rows after stale filter
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `live` filter drops entries where `stale` is true from `rows`, but the header is still built from `entries.length` (all entries, including stale). The manifest text therefore declares `# entry-count: N` while emitting fewer than N data rows. Any consumer that trusts the header to know how many entries/rows to read, size, validate, or paginate (lines[1] `entry-count` vs. line count) now mis-counts: it will expect rows that were never written. Pre-change, count == row count, so this is a regression introduced by the filter; the change silently redefines `rows` without updating the count contract.

findings.title: Fix entry-count header to match filtered live rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The new filter drops stale entries from `rows`, but line 22 still emits `headerLines(opts, entries.length)` using the unfiltered array. Before this change, rows and count were both `entries.length`, so the header `# entry-count: N` always equaled the number of tab-delimited data rows. Now, for any input with `stale` entries, the header reports a count larger than the number of rows actually emitted, so any consumer that parses `entry-count` to size/slice the row list (or uses it as a data-integrity check) sees a contradiction: count > rows, and the missing rows are silently attributed to truncation/corruption rather than intentional filtering.

Because the symbol is exported, the broken behavior is part of the module's public surface, not gated by any caller-side check in this repo.

findings.title: stop replacing execute body with an unconditional throw

findings.title: execute() unconditionally throws, breaking its string contract

findings.title: canProceed payment gate blocks saving unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared predicate read by two distinct actions: submitOrder (@src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (@src/actions.ts:9). Order.state !== "ready" only requires a draft state, and the newly-added `order.payment === "paid"` legitimately governs submission but not draft persistence. For a draft with payment="missing" (state="draft"), the predicate now returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked" (@src/actions.ts:9) instead of "saved" — a legitimately approvable action is rejected by a gate that should not govern it. This is a Trigger A over-block regression: a user editing a draft cannot save it until it is paid.

Every page loses its last row, and summarize() therefore omits one row per page from the rendered output, contradicting page_window's own docstring ('Rows belonging to page_index') and _window_bounds' stated half-open [start, end) contract.

findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open end (end = min(start+page_size, row_count)), so valid positions are start..end-1. The rewritten loop uses range(start, end - 1), which stops at end-2 and silently omits the last row of every page. With page_size=2 and 4 rows, page 0 renders only row 1 instead of rows 1-2; with page_size=1 every page is empty (range(start, start)). render_page and summarize inherit this, so rendered output loses data on every page boundary.

findings.title: Fix off-by-one: page_window drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) range (end = min(start+page_size, row_count)), and page_window iterates range(start, end - 1), so it never includes index end-1. Every page silently loses its final row. For rows=[a,b,c,d,e], page_size=2: page 0 -> range(0,1) -> [a] (expected [a,b]); page 1 -> range(2,3) -> [c] (expected [c,d]); page 2 -> range(4,4) -> [] (expected [e]). render_page then emits fewer numbered lines (and an empty page for the last one), and summarize joins those truncated pages, so displayed data is dropped and pagination is wrong. This is a regression: the base version used range(start, end).

findings.title: Inverted TTL check serves expired values and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was inverted from `<` to `>`. `Date.now() - entry.storedAt` is the entry's AGE. With `>` the code only returns entry.value when age > ttlMs, i.e. only when the entry is EXPIRED, and it deletes the entry + returns null when the entry is still FRESH (age < ttlMs). Every cached read therefore either returns stale data past its TTL or throws away a valid entry, defeating the cache entirely.

findings.title: pruneDone skips jobs and mutates its input array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing elements with `splice` while iterating with `forEach` shifts subsequent elements down, so the index advanced by forEach skips the element right after each removal. With two adjacent done jobs (e.g. [{done:true},{done:true}]) the second is never visited and survives the prune, so the function returns an array that still contains done jobs. It also mutates the caller's array in place, whereas the previous `filter` returned a new array, changing observable behavior for callers holding the original reference.

findings.title: Invert TTL condition: fresh entries dropped, expired values served
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, `get` returned `entry.value` while `Date.now() - storedAt < ttlMs` (entry still fresh) and otherwise deleted the expired entry and returned null. The new condition `> this.ttlMs` returns the value only when the entry is already EXPIRED, and for a fresh entry falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null;`. A value just `set()` (age 0) is always `0 > ttlMs` = false, so it is immediately deleted and `get` returns null; conversely an entry older than the TTL is served as if valid. The cache is fully inverted — it never returns fresh values and serves stale ones.

findings.title: splice-during-forEach skips adjacent done jobs and mutates input
findings.whyItBreaks: Iterating with `forEach` while calling `jobs.splice(index, 1)` shrinks the array under the iterator, so the element shifted into the removed slot is never visited. For `jobs = [{done:true},{done:true}]`: index 0 splices → array is `[{done:true}]`; the loop's next index 1 is past the end, so the second done job survives and is returned. The original `.filter(job => !job.done)` removed all done jobs and returned a new array; the new version also mutates the caller's array in place (aliasing/for-each side effects) rather than returning a copy.

findings.title: Restore TTL freshness check: condition is inverted
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard now returns entry.value when the entry is EXPIRED (age > ttlMs) and deletes the entry + returns null when it is still FRESH (age <= ttlMs). This inverts cache semantics: every get() after insertion but before expiry evicts the valid value and yields null, while stale entries past their TTL are served as if valid. Any consumer of TtlCache receives stale data and loses valid cached values.

findings.title: pruneDone skips done jobs that are adjacent in the array
findings.whyItBreaks: splice(index,1) inside forEach shifts subsequent elements down one index while forEach still advances to index+1, so the element that moved into the removed slot is never visited. Example: [{done:true},{done:true}] → index 0 splices to [{done:true}], loop ends at index 1, leaving one done job unpruned. Any run of consecutive done jobs leaves entries behind, so pruneDone no longer removes all done jobs as its name/contract promises.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a NEW filtered array and left the input untouched. The new implementation splices the passed-in `jobs` array and returns the same reference, so any caller that keeps using its original array (or shares it elsewhere) silently observes removed elements — an unannounced side-effect change to an exported public helper, risking dropped/unexpected queue state in holders of that reference.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard so averageAmount returns 0, not NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard means an empty input now computes 0/0, returning NaN. This silently changes the previously-defined contract (empty set => 0) to a non-numeric value that propagates through any arithmetic, comparison, or display and corrupts downstream aggregation/reporting. This is an exported public function, so the changed contract is the defect regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Avoid mutating caller array in busiest; keep defensive copy

Any caller that reuses `rows` (e.g. for display order, iteration, or a later aggregate over the original order) now observes the array silently reordered by descending amount. This is an exported public function, so the mutation of caller-owned data is a live contract defect even without an in-repo caller.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty input (was 0)
findings.whyItBreaks: The `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard was removed, so `total / rows.length` becomes `0 / 0` = NaN for an empty array. This is an exported function whose prior contract returned 0; NaN silently poisons any downstream arithmetic, display, or aggregation instead of the previous well-defined zero.

findings.title: busiest mutates the caller's array via in-place sort
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation sorted a copy (`[...rows].sort(...)`), leaving the input untouched. The new body calls `rows.sort(...)`, which sorts the caller's array in place as a side effect. Any caller that reuses its `rows` after calling `busiest` (iteration order, later indexing, further processing) now sees a silently reordered array — a behavior change and data mutation of caller-owned input.

findings.title: Removing empty-input guard makes averageAmount([]) return NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard was the only handling of the empty case. With it gone, line 8 computes `total / rows.length` = `0 / 0`, so averageAmount([]) now returns NaN instead of the previously-defined 0. findings.title: busiest mutates caller's array by sorting in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous body sorted a defensive copy via `[...rows].sort(...)`, leaving the argument untouched. The new body calls `rows.sort(...)` directly, so busiest() now reorders the caller's array in place (descending by amount) as a side effect. Any caller that retains or reuses the array it passed (ordering, indexing, subsequent processing) sees corrupted/changed data, while the function's signature/doc give no indication it mutates its argument.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically. For scores with differing digit counts the ordering is wrong (e.g. [2,10] sorts ascending to ["10","2"] -> [10,2], reverse -> [2,10]), so the cutoff selected at src/leaderboard.ts:15 is a non-top value and the filter at :16 keeps/slices the wrong players. Substitute players=[{score:2},{score:10}], n=1: cutoff=2, both pass the filter, slice(0,1) returns the score-2 player instead of the score-10 player. Multi-digit leaderboards (e.g. 9 vs 10, 99 vs 100) silently return the wrong top-N set and wrong formatBoard ordering.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending sort in rankScores (default sort is lexicographic)
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator coerces elements to strings and orders by UTF-16 code units, so ['10','5','9'] sorts ascending to ['10','5','9'] and reverse yields ['9','5','10'] — not numeric descending ['10','9','5']. topPlayers reads scores[min(n,len)-1] as the numeric cutoff (line 15) and filters p.score >= cutoff, so a lexicographically-wrong cutoff selects the wrong players. Concrete failure: topPlayers([{name:'a',score:9},{name:'b',score:10}], 1) → cutoff=9 (lexicographic max), both pass the filter, slice(0,1) returns player 'a' (score 9) instead of player 'b' (score 10). The old code used scores.sort((a,b)=>b-a), which was correct; this is a regression.

findings.title: Default Array.sort is lexicographic, breaking numeric score ranking
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() with no comparator coerces numbers to strings and sorts by UTF-16 code units, so ordering is not numeric. For scores [100, 10, 9]: sort() gives [10, 100, 9], reverse() gives [9, 100, 10]. With n=2, cutoff = scores[1] = 100, filter keeps only [100], and slice returns a single player instead of the top two [100, 10]. Even n>=length drops players: n=3 gives cutoff 10 and omits the score 9. The previous f=(a,b)=>b-a ordering was numerically correct. This regression is observable through the exported topPlayers and its consumer formatBoard (@src/leaderboard.ts:20).

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() now uses Python string `==` instead of `hmac.compare_digest`. `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte and on length, so comparison time varies with how many leading hex characters of a guess match the expected HMAC. An attacker who can submit repeated webhook requests and measure response timing can recover the expected signature byte-by-byte and forge a valid signature, bypassing the auth gate that handle() relies on (`if not verify(...): return {"status": 401}` @app/webhook.py:14). This is a security regression introduced by this PR.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in webhook signature verify
findings.whyItBreaks: The change swaps hmac.compare_digest for the `==` operator. Python str `==` short-circuits on the first differing character, so comparison time depends on the number of matching leading bytes of the attacker-supplied signature. An attacker who can time handle()/verify() responses can recover the expected HMAC byte-by-byte and forge a valid given_signature, bypassing the 401 gate at app/webhook.py:14-15 and reaching processor(payload) with attacker-controlled data. compare_digest was specifically there to prevent this (CWE-208/CWE-347).

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in webhook signature verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() authenticates webhook payloads by comparing the derived hex HMAC against the caller-supplied signature. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits at the first mismatching byte and leaks how many leading bytes match, whereas hmac.compare_digest runs in time independent of content. An attacker who can measure response timing can recover the expected signature byte-by-byte and then forge a valid given_signature, bypassing the 401 gate in handle() and reaching processor(payload) (app/webhook.py:13-16). This is a behavior change on a live authentication path introduced by this diff; the boolean result is otherwise unchanged, so nothing else in the diff masks it.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously all three writes (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) ran inside a single `with db.transaction()` block, so the whole transfer committed or rolled back together. The refactor now runs `_apply_balances(db, ...)` at line 24 AFTER the `with` block at line 22 has exited (committing the ledger INSERT). The two balance UPDATEs are therefore no longer part of the ledger INSERT's transaction, and the debit/credit UPDATEs are no longer atomic with each other. If the process crashes or the second UPDATE raises between the debit and credit, the debit is already committed with no matching credit (money destroyed), or the ledger records a transfer whose balances never changed (phantom transfer). This removes the crash-consistency guarantee the original transaction provided for a financial operation.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change all three writes ran under one `with db.transaction():`, so a failure rolled back everything atomically. Now only `_record_ledger` runs inside the transaction (line 22-23) and `_apply_balances` executes afterwards outside it (line 24). The ledger row is committed first; if either `UPDATE accounts` raises (or the process dies between the two blocks), the transfer is recorded but the sender/recipient balances are not moved, or only the debit applies, leaving the ledger and account balances inconsistent and unrecoverable via rollback. The function's atomic-transfer contract is silently broken on any failure path.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the DB transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The refactor extracted _apply_balances but called it after the `with db.transaction():` block. Now only the ledger INSERT commits in the transaction (app/transfer.py:23); the two balance UPDATEs run afterwards outside any transaction (app/transfer.py:24 -> app/transfer.py:8-16). At base all three statements shared one transaction and rolled back together. With the change, any failure in _apply_balances (constraint error, dropped connection) or a crash between the commit and the updates leaves the ledger recording the transfer while balances are unapplied. Worse, the debit and credit are no longer atomic with each other, so a failure between the two UPDATEs can debit from_acct without crediting to_acct (lost funds). The exception still propagates, but the compensating rollback is gone, so callers cannot recover the now-committed ledger row.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, shifting day boundaries
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous body used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate and returned a deterministic UTC calendar day. The new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate (local time). For a timestamp near a day boundary the returned key differs by the host timezone, e.g. in TZ=America/New_York billingDay(new Date('2024-01-01T03:00:00Z')) now returns '2023-12-31' instead of '2024-01-01', and sameBillingDay classifies two instants across UTC midnight as the same day. Any billing rollup, idempotency key, or per-day aggregation keyed on this value is now server-timezone dependent and can land in the wrong day or double/skip a day under DST.

findings.title: billingDay switched from UTC to local-time date parts
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation used at.getUTCFullYear()/getUTCMonth()/getUTCDate(), so billingDay was anchored to UTC and produced the same string for a given instant regardless of the host/process timezone. The new body uses getFullYear()/getMonth()/getDate(), which read the local timezone of whatever process runs the code. For the same Date the result now varies by process TZ (and by server region, e.g. '2026-01-01T00:30:00Z' becomes '2025-12-31' under a US TZ but '2026-01-01' under UTC), and it also changes across DST. Any persisted/compared billing days (including sameBillingDay below) will silently disagree with days computed under the previous UTC contract, causing mis-bucketed billing periods and off-by-one day charges/aggregations. This is a body-level semantic change to an exported public helper with no accompanying intent in the diff.

findings.title: billingDay no longer computes the UTC day; use of local time breaks day keys
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation built the key from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so billingDay(Date) produced one canonical day string regardless of process/host timezone. The new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate (local timezone), so the returned key now depends on the host TZ. Two effects: (1) sameBillingDay(a, b) — unchanged body at src/billing/day.ts:8 that compares billingDay strings — now returns true/false based on local offsets, so two instants in the same UTC day can compare unequal (e.g. 2026-10-01T23:30Z vs 2026-10-02T00:30Z are equal in UTC but fall on different local days for a TZ east of UTC), and two instants in different UTC days can compare equal for a TZ west of UTC; (2) the emitted key itself changes for any date near a local-midnight boundary, so billing-day keys already persisted/produced by the previous version are no longer reproduced, and the same instant yields different keys on TZ-shifted hosts (local dev vs UTC container).

findings.title: Dropping tenant from memo key leaks cross-tenant profiles
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level `memo` (src/profile.ts:7) is keyed only by `account` after this change, while `memo.set(key, profile)` (src/profile.ts:18) stores the Profile fetched for a specific `tenant`. Two tenants sharing an account string (e.g. `acme:alice` then `globex:alice`) both map to key `alice`, so the second `readProfile` hits `if (cached) return cached;` (src/profile.ts:16) and returns tenant acme's Profile — whose `profile.tenant` is 'acme' — to a caller that requested tenant globex. This silently breaks tenant isolation and, since the wrong object is returned as if valid, a caller cannot distinguish it from a correct fetch. Before this change the key `${tenant}:${account}` kept tenants separate.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, causing cross-tenant profile collision
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile is keyed only by `account` after this change. The previous key `${tenant}:${account}` isolated tenants. With this change, two calls such as readProfile('tenantA','alice',...) and readProfile('tenantB','alice',...) share the memo entry, so the second call returns the first tenant's cached Profile instead of fetching its own — a silent cross-tenant data leak and wrong result. The function's own signature still promises the profile for the given (tenant, account) pair, and fetchProfile is invoked per-tenant, so tenant is clearly part of the identity.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, causing cross-tenant profile collision
findings.whyItBreaks: The key changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account`. `memo` is a single module-level Map shared across all tenants, and `readProfile` reads it via `memo.get(key)` (line 15) and returns the hit (line 16) before calling `fetchProfile`. Two tenants with the same account string therefore share one entry: a call `readProfile('tenantB', 'acct1', f)` after `readProfile('tenantA', 'acct1', f)` returns `tenantA`'s cached Profile (with tenantA's displayName) without fetching, leaking/returning the wrong tenant's profile. Profile.tenant is a field callers will observe as inconsistent with the requested tenant.

findings.title: Stop swallowing missing-key error in exported load()
findings.whyItBreaks: Base `load` threw `Error("missing: "+key)` when a key was absent; the new try/catch discards that signal and returns "". This is an exported public contract (src/store.ts:1), so every caller is forced to conflate a missing key with a legitimately stored empty string. `loadAll` (src/store.ts:12) maps `load` over keys, so a batch containing absent keys now silently yields "" entries instead of surfacing the failure — callers that persist, bill, or report the result act on the fallback as if it were real data. The catch is also a catch-all (`catch {}`), so any future error thrown inside the block is swallowed too.

findings.whyItBreaks: `load` previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")` for an absent key (base line 4). The new catch-all (src/store.ts:6-7) discards that signal and returns `""`, so every caller is now forced to conflate a missing/unresolved value with a real stored empty string. Because `load` is exported (and re-exposed wholesale by `loadAll` at src/store.ts:12, which now returns empty entries instead of throwing), the unusable contract ships to all callers: they can no longer detect absence, and persisting/reporting/branching on the fallback treats failure as real data. The catch also silently absorbs any unexpected throw (e.g. a non-Map store), masking genuine faults.

findings.title: Do not swallow missing-key error in exported load()
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, load() threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when the key was absent (base src/store.ts:3), so callers could not mistake a missing entry for data. The new try/catch (src/store.ts:2-8) is a catch-all that discards that signal and returns "" instead. An empty string is a legitimate stored value, so failure and success become indistinguishable. This is an exported public contract: loadAll (src/store.ts:12) maps over keys and calls load, so a batch containing any missing key now returns a partial array of "" entries that a caller may persist or report as real loaded values, instead of surfacing the failure.

findings.title: Restore timeoutMs: rename silently disables the retry deadline
findings.whyItBreaks: `Config` is exported. The diff removes `timeoutMs` and adds `timeout`, and `retry` now computes `const deadline = Date.now() + config.timeout;` (@src/retry.ts:8). Any existing JS/`any`-typed caller that still passes `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` leaves `config.timeout === undefined`, so `deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN`, and the guard `if (Date.now() > deadline) return;` (@src/retry.ts:10) is `Date.now() > NaN` → always false. The time budget is then silently ignored and the loop runs the full `maxAttempts` with no timeout — a regression versus base, which enforced `timeoutMs`. TS consumers instead get a hard type error on upgrade, so there is no migration path either way.

findings.title: Renaming Config.timeoutMs to timeout breaks callers and silently disables timeout
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported, so renaming the public field timeoutMs→timeout is a breaking change for every existing consumer. A TS caller still passing {timeoutMs} now fails to compile (unknown property); an untyped/compiled caller gets config.timeout === undefined, so deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN at src/retry.ts:8 (and :21). The guard `Date.now() > deadline` at :10 (and :23) compares against NaN, which is always false, so the deadline check never returns early and the timeout is silently ignored — all attempts run with no time bound.

findings.title: retryBackground treats `retries` as total attempts; retries:0 never runs fn

With the natural caller value `retries: 0` ("run once, no retries") the guard `0 < 0` is false and fn is never invoked at all, so the background task silently does nothing. An existing consumer passing {maxAttempts, timeoutMs} yields config.timeout === undefined, so deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN, and the guard `Date.now() > deadline` at line 10 is always false. findings.title: Widening value to number while reading .length breaks build and renders undefined
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 2 widens `value` from `string` to `string | number`, but line 6 computes `value.length`. `number` has no `length` property, so TypeScript rejects the expression (TS2339: Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'), failing compilation for any strict build. At runtime, if a number is passed, `(42).length` is `undefined`, so `label` becomes the literal string "len=undefined" and that bogus value is written into the input's defaultValue — the caller's real value is silently discarded.
