findings.whyItBreaks: The public prop `value: string | number` now advertises that numbers are accepted, but the body computes `value.length`, which is `undefined` for any number, producing the string `len=undefined` (the number's actual content is dropped). As a union-typed property `value.length` is also a TypeScript error (Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'), so the field's declared contract and its implementation disagree.

findings.title: number value renders len=undefined and breaks type-check
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported contract FieldProps.value: string | number promises numeric values are accepted, but the body computes `${value.length}`. For a number, `.length` is undefined, so the rendered label becomes the literal "len=undefined" instead of the numeric value's length (numbers are not strings; `(42).length` is undefined). The same line also fails TS type-check on the union (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'`), so any typed build flags Field.tsx:6. Either the type must stay `string`, or the body must stringify first (e.g. `String(value).length`).

findings.title: Remove step that prints secret TOKEN to workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step injects the repository secret TOKEN via env on a `push`-triggered job and then interpolates it into a shell command (`echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`), writing the secret's plaintext value into the workflow run log. Workflow logs are readable by every user with read access to the repo (and are persisted/exportable), so the deploy credential is disclosed to anyone with repo read access. GitHub's automatic secret masking only redacts exact registered matches on a best-effort basis and does not protect the value once it is echoed, captured by other tooling, or transformed, so it is not a safe mitigation — and the step has no functional purpose beyond printing the secret.

findings.title: Stop echoing the deploy token into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step injects `secrets.TOKEN` as `$TOKEN` and prints it with `echo`, writing the credential into the workflow run log. Actions logs are retained and downloadable by anyone with read access to the repository/Actions, so the deploy token leaks and can be reused to authenticate as the workflow. The step performs no build work — it runs between checkout and `make build` purely to emit the secret.

findings.title: Do not echo secrets.TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step injects ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} via env and prints it with `echo`, so the credential is written into the GitHub Actions run log. GitHub's `::add-mask::` redaction is a log-scrubbing heuristic, not an access boundary: the value is still emitted into the log stream, survives in raw logs/artifacts, and is exposed whenever the printed string is transformed or the log is forwarded to an aggregator that does not apply masking. Exposing a deploy credential provides no deploy value (the actual deploy is `make build`) while enlarging the credential's exposure surface.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer to avoid 1 MiB diff failures
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1024*1024. The full patch is produced by `git diff <mergeBase> <headSha>` (line 140) through this helper; when that output exceeds 1 MiB, spawnSync kills the child, sets res.error=ENOBUFS and res.status=null, so the guard at line 38 (res.status !== 0) throws. runGithub's catch (line 182) then posts a failing 'review failed' check and never runs the review. gh()/ghText() still allow 64 MiB (lines 19, 29), so the cap here is an unintended 64x reduction that silently breaks the primary workflow for large PRs (lockfiles, generated code, big refactors).

findings.title: git() lost its 64 MiB maxBuffer, aborting large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` falls back to Node's spawnSync default of 1 MiB. `git diff mergeBase headSha` (line 140) and `git diff --name-only` routinely exceed 1 MiB on PRs touching lockfiles or generated code. When the cap is exceeded the child is killed and spawnSync sets result.error (ENOBUFS) with status === null; `res.status !== 0` is then true, so git() throws `git diff ... failed:` with an empty/truncated stderr. The whole review crashes and posts a 'review failed' check for exactly the large PRs that most need review, whereas the previous 64 MiB limit handled them.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() or large PRs fail the review
findings.whyItBreaks: The only sizeable git() caller is `patch = git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)` (src/adapters/github.ts:140), which returns the entire diff text. Node's spawnSync default maxBuffer is 1024*1024 (1MiB); the base revision explicitly raised it to 64MiB. When stdout exceeds the cap, spawnSync kills the child, sets `res.error` (ENOBUFS) and leaves `res.status === null`, so the `res.status !== 0` branch at line 38 throws (with empty/truncated stderr). runGithub's catch then posts a failure check-run (lines 184-193) and exits 1, so any PR with a diff larger than ~1MiB — trivial for lockfiles or generated files — is reported as 'review failed' and blocked, a regression versus base.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox flag on codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (the checkout under review). The removed `-s read-only` was the only thing forcing the agent's sandbox policy: `-s` becomes `ConfigOverrides.sandbox_mode` (codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs:288,328-332) and overrides `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml`. Without it, `sandbox_mode` resolves from ambient config; `SandboxMode::default()` is ReadOnly (codex-rs/protocol/src/config_types.rs:104-107), so a default config is unaffected, but any user config `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"`/`"danger-full-access"`, a permission profile, or a layered `$CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml` now takes effect. In those environments the review agent can write to and execute model-generated commands against the repository being reviewed — breaking the explicit read-only guarantee this code asserted and risking mutation/corruption of the reviewed checkout.

findings.title: Restore `-s read-only` so the spawned codex cannot modify files
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change the spawned `codex exec` was explicitly pinned to the `read-only` sandbox (`-s read-only`), guaranteeing the reviewing agent could not modify the workspace or anywhere else on disk. The change removes that flag, so sandbox policy now falls back to the user's `~/.codex` default sandbox_mode and the CLI's own default. For any environment where that default is `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access`, the subagent — which is fed the repo under review as prompt/context, i.e. attacker-controllable input (prompt injection surface) — can now write to the repo and, in the full-access case, the host filesystem. The reviewer is also documented elsewhere as a read-only reviewer, so this silently changes its safety contract while the returned string (`out`) still looks identical, hiding the fact that side effects occurred.

findings.title: Restore forced read-only sandbox for codex exec subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `-s read-only` was a CLI-level override that forced the spawned `codex exec` into a read-only sandbox regardless of the user's global Codex config. `codex exec` loads `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` (that is why `--ignore-user-config` exists) and honors `sandbox_mode` from it; the `-s` flag has higher precedence. Without the flag, a developer whose global config sets `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` (or `"danger-full-access"`) now has the review agent run model-generated commands with write/full access against `opts.repoPath` — the untrusted repository under review — instead of the previously guaranteed read-only execution.

findings.title: Restore merge-base so PR diff excludes base-branch-only changes
findings.whyItBreaks: `baseSha` comes from `PR_BASE_SHA` (the base branch tip) at line 138. When the base branch has advanced past the fork point and the checkout is the PR head rather than a merge commit, `git diff baseSha HEAD` (two-dot) contains every base-branch-only commit as reversed hunks, so `patch` and `changedFiles` cover files the PR never touched. The review then sees non-PR changes (e.g. spurious deletions) and `changedPaths` gains base-only files, so `inlineComments` (line 63) can emit comments for paths outside the PR diff; GitHub rejects that payload with 422 and the catch at line 96 silently re-posts the review with NO inline comments. Precondition substitution: baseSha = a commit on the base branch not in HEAD's ancestry, HEAD = PR head -> diff = PR changes + reversed base changes (wrong), whereas merge-base(baseSha, headSha)..headSha yields only PR changes. The old merge-base was the guard against exactly this; the no-env fallback path (baseSha already = merge-base(origin/main, HEAD)) is unaffected, which is why this only bites on the CI env path.

findings.title: PR diff no longer uses merge-base/named PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: Base computed patch = git diff(mergeBase, headSha) and changedFiles from mergeBase, where mergeBase = git merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and headSha = PR_HEAD_SHA || rev-parse HEAD. The new code diff()s baseSha against the literal WORKTREE HEAD and derives changedFiles from baseSha. Two concrete effects when the env vars this function exists for (guarded by 'must run in Actions') are set: (1) HEAD literal replaces headSha, so when PR_HEAD_SHA != local HEAD (the default actions/checkout on a pull_request event is the refs/pull/N/merge commit) the patch/changedFiles describe a different revision than headSha, which is still used as the review commit_id at line 85 and check head_sha at line 124 — the review content and the reported revision disagree, and inline comments anchored via changedPaths (line 63) can target lines that are not in that commit; (2) removing the merge-base reduction means that when PR_BASE_SHA is the base-branch tip (github.event.pull_request.base.sha, the normal CI meaning), git diff baseSha..HEAD is a two-dot diff that includes every commit merged into the base branch after the PR forked, so unrelated files enter changedFiles/patch and are reviewed/attributed to this PR. The old mergeBase line existed precisely to avoid that, and it is dead weight only if PR_BASE_SHA were already a merge base.

findings.title: Diff PR against merge base, not raw base tip
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch and the changed-file set are now produced with a two-dot diff `baseSha..HEAD`. Previously the code first computed `git merge-base baseSha headSha` and diffed from that common ancestor. `baseSha` is `PR_BASE_SHA` (the base branch tip) or `merge-base origin/main HEAD`; when the base branch has advanced past the PR's fork point and HEAD is the PR head commit, `git diff baseSha HEAD` additionally contains the reverse of every base-branch-only commit landed since the fork. The reviewer then sees and comments on changes this PR never made, and `changedPaths` (built from the same two-dot range, used to filter inline comments at src/adapters/github.ts:61-70) no longer matches the PR's actual files.

findings.title: String replacement reinterprets `$` in JSON/patch, corrupting prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: Passing a function as `String.prototype.replace`'s second argument inserts its return value literally. The pre-PR code intentionally used `() => JSON.stringify(...)` / `() => bundle.patch` for exactly this reason. Replacing the callbacks with plain strings makes the replacement subject to `$` substitution patterns: `$$` collapses to `$`, `$&` expands to the matched placeholder (e.g. the literal text `{{PATCH}}`), and `` $` ``, `$'`, `$1`...$99, `$<name>` expand to surrounding/group text. `bundle.patch` is arbitrary raw diff text and the JSON blobs are arbitrary repo/patch content, so any patch containing shell variables (`$X`), template literals (`${...}`), regex/`$1` backrefs, or jQuery (`$(...)`) will silently mangle the prompt sent to the model — e.g. a `$&` in the patch injects the placeholder `{{PATCH}}` and can drop the real patch body, so the critic reviews corrupted or missing content instead of an error.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to avoid `$`-pattern prompt corruption
findings.whyItBreaks: With a string replacement value, String.prototype.replace interprets special patterns in the replacement text: `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched literal (`{{PATCH}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`), `` $` ``→the entire preceding template, and `$'`→the entire trailing template. The base revision used replacer functions (`() => ...`), whose return value is inserted literally, precisely avoiding this. The patch and findings JSON are arbitrary reviewed content: a diff touching a shell script, Makefile, or sed/awk command routinely contains `$$` (PID) or `$&`, so the critic prompt is silently mangled before being sent to the model. The same defect applies to line 25 (`{{BUNDLE}}`, whose JSON embeds `bundle.patch`).

findings.title: Restore literal replacers: `$` in bundle/patch is now substituted
findings.whyItBreaks: Base used function replacers (`() => JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)`, `() => bundle.patch`) which insert their return value literally. Head passes the raw strings directly, and String.prototype.replace interprets `$`-patterns inside a string replacement: `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched text, `` $` ``→the prompt prefix, `$'`→the prompt suffix. So when `bundle`, the JSON-stringified `candidate`, or `bundle.patch` contains `$&` (common in patch/diff text and shell/regex code), `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}` is replaced by the literal placeholder, silently dropping the real content the model must review; `` $` ``/`$'` instead splice the entire surrounding prompt template in, producing a corrupted review prompt. The search strings are plain (no capture groups) so `$1`/`$<name>` stay literal, but `$$`, `$&`, `` $` `` and `$'` do not — this is a genuine regression from the deliberately literal base behavior.

findings.title: Re-add commit_id to fallback review so it stays pinned to headSha
findings.whyItBreaks: The JSON primary path still pins the review with commit_id (src/adapters/github.ts:88-93) and the check run pins head_sha (src/adapters/github.ts:124-133), but the fallback gh call now sends only event/body. GitHub defaults a review with no commit_id to the PR's most recent commit, so when the fallback fires while the PR head has moved past the reviewed SHA (or headSha is not the current tip, e.g. a re-run/stale PR_HEAD_SHA), the verdict is recorded against a commit that was never reviewed and disagrees with the check run for the same run.

findings.title: normalizeFinding fabricates defaults instead of rejecting malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Every per-field guard was deleted and replaced with coercing fallbacks: invalid/missing severity -> "P1", invalid/missing category -> "bug", missing file -> "", missing title -> "Untitled finding", missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix -> "", lineStart -> 0 and lineEnd -> Number(raw.lineEnd ?? raw.lineStart ?? 0) (0, or NaN for non-numeric input such as "abc"). The only caller, normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:131), previously propagated normalizeFinding's throws in strict mode and dropped invalid entries in non-strict mode; both the strict default and the `strict=false` drop-and-filter branch were removed, so there is now no path that can reject or discard a malformed finding. A malformed model entry is silently reported/persisted as a real, well-formed finding with a non-empty title and an escalated P1 severity, and failure is indistinguishable from a legitimate value at every downstream decision point.

findings.title: Restore validation in normalizeFinding; silent coercion hides malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously threw on every malformed input (`malformed finding: not an object|invalid severity|invalid category|missing file|missing title|missing whyItBreaks|missing suggestedFix|invalid lineStart|invalid lineEnd`), so callers of the exported normalizeReview could distinguish garbage LLM output from a real finding. The new body discards all of those signals: a finding with no `file` becomes `file: ""`, an empty `whyItBreaks`/`suggestedFix` becomes `""`, a missing/zero/negative `lineStart` becomes `0`, and a non-numeric `lineStart` becomes `NaN` (line 104-105, `Number(raw.lineStart ?? 0)` with no Number.isFinite guard), while an unrecognized severity is silently reported as `"P1"` (line 98) and an unrecognized category as `"bug"` (line 100-102). A reviewer/consumer using `lineStart: 0` or `NaN` with `file: ""` to anchor an inline comment will post it at an invalid location, and a garbled entry is now surfaced as a legitimate P1 instead of being rejected. The removal of the `strict` parameter (line 113) also deletes the previous non-strict path that dropped invalid findings, so no caller can filter them anymore.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of defaulting severity/file/line to P1/""/0
findings.whyItBreaks: The rewritten normalizeFinding discards every validation the base version performed and maps malformed input to plausible real-looking values: an absent/invalid severity becomes "P1", an invalid category becomes "bug", a missing file becomes "", and missing/invalid lineStart/lineEnd become 0 (or NaN for non-numeric input, since the base `Number.isFinite(...)`/`> 0` guards were deleted and replaced by bare `Number(...)`). Previously these cases threw (`malformed finding: ...` at base schema.ts:97-122) or, in non-strict mode, the finding was dropped (base schema.ts:157-165). A garbled finding that still carries a valid `confidence` (e.g. 0.9) now passes any downstream confidence gate and is surfaced as a legitimate blocking P1 finding anchored at file "" line 0/NaN, so callers can no longer distinguish "the model emitted a finding" from "the output was malformed and we papered over it" — the failure signal is gone (TRIGGER D).

findings.title: Restore explicit repo in `gh pr view` ref resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (line 42-46), so on a clean/ephemeral self-hosted runner the workspace is not yet a git repo and has no origin remote. `gh` resolves the target repo from `-R`/`--repo`, the `GH_REPO` env var, or the cwd's git remotes; gh 2.98.0 does not read `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` (verified: that literal is absent from the binary, while `no git remotes found` and `failed to determine base repo: %w` are present). With `-R "$REPO"` and the `REPO` env removed, `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` fails here with `failed to determine base repo: no git remotes found`. Because the failure happens inside `$(...)` and only the `echo` exit status matters, the step still reports success and writes `head=` / `base=` (empty). Downstream, `actions/checkout` then falls back to the default branch (empty `ref`) and `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` are empty, so a manual workflow_dispatch review silently runs against the wrong revision instead of the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo target for gh pr view before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: These two lines are the only ones that use `gh pr view` (the `if [ -n "$EVENT_HEAD" ]` branch is skipped for `pull_request`, so this path is exactly `workflow_dispatch`). The step runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (line 42), so the workspace is not a git repo yet; `gh` now has no `-R`, no `GH_REPO` env (step env is only GH_TOKEN + the PR/EVENT vars), and does not read `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` (verified locally: `cd /tmp && GH_TOKEN=dummy GITHUB_REPOSITORY=o/r gh pr view 7 --json headRefOid` → `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository`). gh therefore fails, the `$( )` substitution yields an empty string, and because the failing command is inside `echo "head=$(...)"` the default `bash -e` errexit does not fire — the step succeeds while writing `head=` and `base=` empty into $GITHUB_OUTPUT. Downstream, `ref: ${{ steps.refs.outputs.head }}` (line 45) is empty so checkout silently falls back to the triggering ref (default branch) instead of the PR head, and `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (lines 56-57) are passed empty to the CLI: the manual review runs against the wrong revision. On a self-hosted runner whose `_work` workspace still holds a clone of a DIFFERENT repo, gh instead silently resolves that repo's origin and fetches the PR number from the wrong repository.

findings.title: Restore --repo in pre-checkout gh pr view calls
findings.whyItBreaks: These two lines run in the `Resolve PR refs` step, which executes BEFORE `actions/checkout` (step starts at line 42). Dropping `-R "$REPO"` (and the `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}` env at old line 30) leaves gh with no way to identify the target repo: gh CLI resolves the repo only from `GH_REPO`, `--repo/-R`, or a git remote in the cwd, and does NOT read `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` (verified: `strings gh` v2.98.0 contains no GITHUB_REPOSITORY reference; it errors with "a repository is required; re-run in a repository or supply one with --repo owner/name"). In a fresh/clean self-hosted workspace there is no `.git`, so both `gh pr view` calls fail. Because the calls sit inside `$(...)` inside `echo`, their non-zero exit status is discarded — the step still succeeds and appends `head=` / `base=` (empty) to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`. Downstream, `Checkout PR head` gets `ref: ''` (line 45) and the review step gets empty `PR_HEAD_SHA`/`PR_BASE_SHA` (lines 56-57), so a manual `workflow_dispatch` run silently reviews the wrong revision instead of failing loudly. This path is only exercised by `workflow_dispatch` (pull_request sets EVENT_HEAD, taking the line 34 branch).

findings.title: Revert lenient candidate parse that silently drops malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, strict=true) throws on any malformed finding (missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, invalid lineStart/lineEnd). Passing strict=false switches the malformed-finding try/catch on, so the candidate pass silently drops that finding and continues. The candidate list is what feeds the critic at src/core/review.ts:34-36, and a dropped finding is never handed to the critic, so it can never appear in the final findings — the review can return pass while a real blocking finding is lost. Before this change the default (strict=true) made malformed candidate output throw loudly; now the lenient parse hides the failure.

findings.title: Don't parse candidate review with strict=false; it silently drops findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview(raw, strict = true): with strict=false each finding is run through normalizeFinding inside a try/catch that returns null on any throw, and nulls are filtered out; with strict=true (the base behavior) the throw propagates and aborts. normalizeFinding throws on a malformed required field (invalid/missing severity or category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive or inverted lineStart/lineEnd, blocking confidence < 0.7). candidate.findings is the ONLY source of findings (line 35 feeds it to the critic, which can only prune, and line 43 derives the verdict from pruned.findings). So a genuine blocking finding with one malformed field is dropped from candidate.findings, never reaches the critic or pruned.findings, and deriveVerdict (empty findings, no blocks=true residual) returns pass instead of changes_requested. The line 30 guard only checks candidate.summary and candidate.checked.length, so an emptied findings list passes it. This turns the previously loud malformed-output error into a silent fail-open on the review's core gate.

findings.title: Lenient candidate parse silently drops real findings before critic
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview's second parameter is `strict` (default true). In strict mode a malformed required field on any candidate finding throws, so review() aborts at line 29 with "malformed review output…" and the caller sees a loud failure. Passing false switches normalizeReview into its lenient branch, which try/catches each normalizeFinding and filters the failures out (returns null). Because a valid finding with one malformed required field (e.g. a P1 whose lineEnd<lineStart, or confidence 0.5, or missing suggestedFix) now parses as null, it is removed from candidate.findings. Those findings are the sole input to the critic (review.ts:35), so the critic never sees the dropped defect, pruned.findings omits it, and deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, …) @review.ts:43 can return "pass" for a PR that strict parsing would have refused to verdict at all. The failure signal (malformed model output) is indistinguishable from a legitimate empty result.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed-output errors as empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: This public/exported function previously threw on malformed input (not an object, non-string summary, missing/non-array findings/checked/residual_risks). It now returns a default-shaped review `{summary: "", findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: []}` for every one of those failure modes. A caller can no longer distinguish 'the review output was malformed/truncated' from 'a legitimately empty review', and an empty review for a review agent is the shape that reads as a clean pass (no findings, nothing to check), so a parse/truncation failure is silently upgraded into a passing verdict instead of an error. The swallow is on the exported API surface, so the unusable contract is itself the defect even though no in-repo caller exercises it yet.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed-output errors into empty defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously normalizeReview threw on bad input (not an object, missing/non-string summary, missing findings/checked/residual_risks arrays), so the caller learned the model output was unusable. The new body turns every failure into a plausible value: summary -> "", findings -> [], checked -> [], residual_risks -> []. A malformed output (e.g. the model returned prose, a null, or a stringified JSON blob) now normalizes to a review with no findings, which downstream verdict logic can read as "no defects / pass" and merge unreviewed code. Failure is no longer distinguishable from a legitimately empty review, so this exported API contract forces every caller to conflate the two.

findings.title: Keep an error signal for malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: The change removes every guard from normalizeReview and replaces them with silent defaults: `raw?.findings` → [] (schema.ts:115-117), `raw?.residual_risks` → [] (schema.ts:118-123), `raw?.summary` → "" (schema.ts:125), `raw?.checked` → [] (schema.ts:127). Previously non-object input, a non-string summary, or missing findings/checked/residual_risks arrays threw. Now `normalizeReview(null)`, `normalizeReview({})`, or any hallucinated/partial model object returns {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]} — a value identical to a real review that legitimately found nothing and blocked nothing. Any consumer that derives a verdict from 'no findings + no blocking residual_risks' will report a clean pass for a failed/truncated/malformed model response, so the failure signal is permanently lost at the source.

findings.title: Restore PR-ref resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed "Resolve PR refs" step used `gh pr view` to derive head/base/base_ref when the event is workflow_dispatch, where `github.event.pull_request` is null. The new code uses `github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` (line 29), so manual dispatch checks out whatever ref the operator selected (typically refs/heads/main), not the requested PR's head. It also drops BASE_REF to the `|| 'main'` fallback (line 35) even when the target PR's base is another branch, and passes empty `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (lines 45-46). The `on.workflow_dispatch` trigger and `if:` condition (lines 10-14, 24) explicitly keep manual dispatch as a supported path, so this is a live-path regression: the review runs against the wrong commit and with empty SHAs. The pull_request path is unaffected (event fields are populated).

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch before merge
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the `Resolve PR refs` step whose `else` branch queried `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid,baseRefOid,baseRef` for non-pull_request events. On `workflow_dispatch`, `github.event.pull_request` is empty, so: (1) the checkout `ref` at line 29 falls back to `github.ref` — the branch the dispatch ran on (default branch), NOT the PR head; (2) `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (lines 45-46) become empty strings; (3) `BASE_REF` (line 35) defaults to `'main'` regardless of the PR's real base. The job still runs on this path (`if:` line 24 includes `github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'`) and the step still consumes `github.event.inputs.pr_number` (line 47), so manual dispatch is a live supported route that now reviews the wrong commit / missing refs. The old `pull_request` path is equivalent only because `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`/`base.sha` are populated there.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: The job still supports workflow_dispatch (line 10-14, required input pr_number; job if at line 24 explicitly allows it), but the deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step was the ONLY place that resolved head/base SHAs via `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` for manual runs. The replacements read only the pull_request payload: on a workflow_dispatch there is no pull_request event, so `github.event.pull_request.base.sha` / `head.sha` (lines 45-46) evaluate to empty strings, and the checkout `ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` (line 29) falls back to `github.ref` — the branch the workflow file runs from (e.g. refs/heads/main), not the reviewed PR's head commit. Likewise 'Fetch base branch' (line 33-35) defaults BASE_REF to `main` since base.ref is absent. Net effect: a manual dispatch no longer supplies the base/head SHAs the tool previously received, and checks out the base branch instead of the PR head; the input description at line 13 still promises 'PR number to review (manual trigger; bypasses pull_request webhook)'.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer or large PR diffs abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is the primary data path for runLocal: patch = git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd) at src/adapters/local.ts:100 (and name-only at :101) is fed straight into the review bundle. Removing maxBuffer reverts spawnSync to Node's default of 1MiB. When git emits more than that, spawnSync kills the child (SIGTERM), sets status=null and error.code='ENOBUFS' (verified: 1,114,112 bytes captured then ENOBUFS). Because status !== 0, the guard at :12-14 throws `git diff ... failed:` with empty stderr, and that throw is not caught in runLocal, so the whole review aborts on any PR whose diff exceeds ~1MB (common with lockfiles, generated code, minified assets, snapshots). At base the 64MB buffer handled these.

findings.title: Restore large maxBuffer on git diff capture
findings.whyItBreaks: git() runs `git diff baseSha HEAD` (src/adapters/local.ts:100) and returns its stdout, so the captured patch is unbounded PR-sized text. Removing maxBuffer falls back to Node's default of 1 MiB. When the diff exceeds 1 MiB, spawnSync terminates the child with ENOBUFS, res.status becomes null and stdout is truncated; since `res.status !== 0` is true, the helper throws at src/adapters/local.ts:12-14 with an empty stderr message. runLocal then rejects before review() ever runs, so any large PR can no longer be reviewed at all (previously supported up to 64 MiB). The sibling gh() call at src/adapters/local.ts:33-36 still sets maxBuffer, confirming the large-output limit was intentional.

findings.title: Restoring 64 MiB git buffer; default 1 MiB breaks large-diff reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is the only way the adapter reads repository data, and its largest output is the full patch itself: `const patch = git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd)` at src/adapters/local.ts:100. With no maxBuffer, spawnSync falls back to Node's 1 MiB limit (verified: output > 1 MiB yields {status:null, signal:'SIGTERM', error:'ENOBUFS'} with stdout truncated at ~1 MiB). Any diff exceeding 1 MiB therefore sets res.status to null, so the `res.status !== 0` guard at line 12 throws `git diff <base> HEAD failed: ` with an empty/truncated stderr — the tool fails on exactly the large PRs it exists to review, where it previously handled up to 64 MiB. Note the sibling gh() helper at lines 33-37 keeps maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64, confirming the removal here is inconsistent with the intended behavior.

findings.title: Downgrading errored review to neutral makes the gate pass
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch block the check run is now posted with conclusion "neutral" (was "failure") while its summary still asserts "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR". GitHub required status checks treat a neutral conclusion as passing, so when review() throws (LLM/API error, parse failure, etc.) the Needlefish check now shows green and no longer blocks the PR — the failure signal is downgraded from blocking to non-blocking, silently converting an unusable review into an approved-looking gate. The human-readable text and the machine-readable conclusion contradict each other, and only the conclusion drives branch protection.

findings.title: Restore failure conclusion so an errored review still blocks merge
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block downgraded the posted check-run conclusion from "failure" to "neutral" while the summary text still says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR". GitHub treats neutral conclusions as passing for required status checks, so when review() throws (model error, gh failure, bad payload) the Needlefish required check is no longer failing and branch protection no longer blocks the merge. Failure and the fallback value are no longer distinguishable to the merge gate, and the fallback is acted on as if the review had produced a legitimate non-blocking verdict (the same value used for needs_human at line 53). This defeats the entire gate: an unreviewed/errored PR can now be merged.

findings.title: Revert errored-review check conclusion back to failure
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch block still prints `Review errored and did NOT pass this PR`, but the check-run conclusion was changed from `failure` to `neutral`. GitHub maps the check-run conclusion `neutral` to a successful status, and a required status check passes on success/skipped/neutral. So when `review()` throws (the exact case where nothing was verified), the previously-blocking `Needlefish` check now reports as passing and the PR becomes mergeable with no successful review, contradicting the summary text the same call emits.

findings.title: Review tool now runs from untrusted PR head; PR can bypass its own gate
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the reviewer was checked out separately from the trusted `frankekn/needlefish@main` (isolated at `path: needlefish`) and only the PR content was untrusted at `target/`. This diff deletes that trusted checkout (removed `Checkout trusted tool (main)`, `path: target`, and the `working-directory` splits), so the single `Checkout PR head` (ref = `steps.refs.outputs.head`, lines 43-47) is now both the reviewed content AND the tool: line 51 runs `pnpm install` from the PR's own package.json/lockfile, and line 59 runs the PR's own `src/cli.ts` as the reviewer while `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` (pull-requests: write, checks: write) is exported into it (lines 55-58) on a `self-hosted` runner. A PR can therefore (a) rewrite `src/cli.ts` to emit/post an approving review and satisfy the very required check that gates the merge, and/or (b) add a malicious dependency/lifecycle script that executes arbitrary code with the repo-scoped token and can persist on the shared self-hosted runner. The `if` guard (line 24) only filters forks, so any same-repo branch author can do this. This reintroduces exactly the risk the deleted comment ('This prevents a PR from controlling its own review') declared the old design avoided.

findings.title: Review tool is executed from the untrusted PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes the 'Checkout trusted tool (main)' step and now only checks out the PR head (lines 43-47), then installs and runs that checkout's own tool: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 51) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 59), with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` under `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write` (lines 16-19, 56). Previously the reviewer was checked out from the trusted `frankekn/needlefish@main` and the PR head was only read as a diff target in `target/`, i.e. never executed. Now a same-repo PR can edit `src/cli.ts` (or the lockfile/postinstall scripts) to emit a PASS review, suppress findings, or run arbitrary code with the write-scoped token — the PR controls its own review gate. The removed comment explicitly stated this pattern 'prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool'; the new code reintroduces exactly that. The `if:` gate (line 24) excludes fork PRs, so exploitability requires a branch in the same repo, but review is the merge gate and this bypasses it.

findings.title: Stop running the PR head's own code as the review tool
findings.whyItBreaks: The base workflow deliberately used a trusted-tool pattern: it checked out the PR head into `target` and a separate copy of the tool from `frankekn/needlefish@main` into `needlefish`, then ran the trusted copy (`$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/needlefish/src/cli.ts`) against the untrusted target. This PR deletes the second checkout entirely and runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from the PR-head checkout itself (line 59), with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` in the environment (line 56) and `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` permissions (lines 18-19) on a `self-hosted` runner. A same-repo PR (the only kind admitted by the `if` guard on line 24) can therefore edit `src/cli.ts` so the reviewer emits a forged PASS/approve for its own change, or exfiltrate/abuse the token, defeating the independence the review gate exists to provide. This is exactly the attack the removed comment block described and guarded against.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported `normalizeFinding` is named and was written to NORMALIZE a raw finding: the base body computed `sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and validated `sev`. The new body feeds `raw.severity` straight into `SEVERITIES.includes(...)`, so case/whitespace variants such as "p1", " p2" or "P0 " that previously normalized now fail the exact-match membership test and fall through to the default bucket. `normalizeReview` (@src/shared/schema.ts:132) is the pass-through caller and relies on this function to return a valid Severity, so realistic model output with casing/whitespace variance is now mis-normalized where it previously was not.

findings.title: Unknown severity silently floored to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The fallback for a missing/unrecognized severity changed from "P1" (base line 97) to "P3" (head line 99). P3 is the lowest priority tier, so a finding whose severity cannot be parsed (e.g. "critical", or any casing/whitespace variant per the normalization change above) is silently persisted/reported as P3 instead of being surfaced or rejected. Callers can no longer distinguish a genuinely low-severity finding from a parse failure, and any downstream gate that blocks on P0/P1 will silently pass these findings. This is the exported public contract of `Finding.severity`, so the conflation ships even with no other in-repo caller.

findings.title: Stop silently downgrading unnormalized/unknown severities to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` forced case/whitespace normalization and mapped anything unrecognized to the conservative default `P1`. The new code tests `raw.severity` directly against ["P0","P1","P2","P3"], so any lowercase/padded/mixed-case severity in the untrusted model JSON (e.g. "p0", " P1 ") now fails the membership check and silently becomes "P3". The fallback for a missing/unknown severity was also changed from "P1" to "P3". Net effect: findings that should be P0/P1 (or that previously defaulted to P1) are demoted to P3, the least severe value — a silent severity downgrade on a public, merge-gating contract in `normalizeFinding`/`normalizeReview`.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization dropped in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version computed `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before the SEVERITIES check, so raw model output such as "p1", "p0" or " P2 " normalized to a valid token. Head compares `raw.severity` verbatim, so any case/whitespace variant now fails `SEVERITIES.includes(...)` and is replaced by the default. Because severity drives how the review pipeline prioritizes and acts on findings, a genuinely valid "p0"/"p1" (security/data-loss) is silently relabeled. The default also moved from "P1" to "P3", so even a missing severity is now treated as lowest priority, further hiding unrecognized findings.

findings.title: Restores GH token leakage into spawned codex child env
findings.whyItBreaks: The change deletes the `env` copy plus `delete env.GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN` and stops passing `env` to `spawnSync`. With `env` omitted, Node defaults to inheriting the full `process.env`, so the `codex exec` child (which runs an autonomous agent over the untrusted PR prompt and can execute read-only shell commands and return their output via `--output-last-message`) now sees and can surface those credentials. A prompt-injected diff can direct the child to emit `env`, and the secret lands in `out` (returned to the caller / logs). This is exactly the exposure the deleted lines existed to prevent.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing before spawning codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the code copied process.env and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, then passed that sanitized `env` to spawnSync. The diff removes both the deletions and the `env` option, so spawnSync falls back to its default and the spawned `codex exec` process (and any tool/subprocess it runs) inherits the full parent environment including those GitHub credentials. The codex subprocess is driven by an attacker-influenceable prompt, so the PR review pipeline can now leak repository-scoped GitHub tokens to the model subprocess.

findings.title: Restore credential scrubbing for spawned codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code built `const env = { ...process.env }`, deleted GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and passed that sanitized object as `env` to spawnSync. This diff removes both the deletions and the `env` option, so `spawnSync` falls back to inheriting the full parent environment. The child is `codex exec` invoked over an attacker-influenced PR review prompt (prompt text + diff are passed via `input`), and codex runs model-directed shell commands with network enabled; the parent's GitHub tokens are therefore handed to a process that untrusted diff content can steer, enabling credential exfiltration (e.g. `env`/`printenv` piped out). Nothing in `codex exec` requires these GitHub tokens, so there is no legitimate reason to re-expose them.

findings.title: Restore fork guard so untrusted PR code can't run on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The worked predicate `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was deleted, so the `review` job now runs for PRs whose head repo differs from the base repo (forks). The job checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (attacker-controlled), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (executes the PR's prepare/postinstall lifecycle scripts) and then `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (runs the PR's own source). On `runs-on: self-hosted` this is arbitrary code execution from an untrusted fork on persistent infrastructure — the classic pwn-request pattern. The old guard existed precisely because forks are a real trigger surface (job is `pull_request`-scoped, `runs-on: self-hosted`). Note the change also fails its apparent purpose: on fork PRs GitHub downgrades `GITHUB_TOKEN` to read-only, so the `--github` comment-post step would fail anyway while still executing untrusted code.

findings.title: Dropped fork guard runs untrusted PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The job-level `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only control restricting this workflow to same-repository PRs. With it removed, the `pull_request` workflow now runs for fork PRs too, and it checks out untrusted head code (`ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, line ~22) and executes it on a `runs-on: self-hosted` runner: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line ~28) runs attacker-supplied dependency lifecycle/postinstall scripts, and `tsx src/cli.ts` (line ~33) runs the PR's own source. This is arbitrary code execution by any external fork author on the self-hosted runner, which is explicitly the untrusted-fork risk the guard existed to prevent.

findings.title: Removing fork guard runs untrusted PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` makes the `review` job run for fork PRs too. The job checks out the PR head from the fork (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (executes dependency lifecycle/install scripts from the PR-controlled lockfile) and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (executes the PR's own source) on a `runs-on: self-hosted` runner. Any external contributor can therefore get arbitrary code execution on persistent CI infrastructure. This guard's only purpose was to keep fork PRs off that runner.

findings.title: Zero duration override now silently replaced by fallback default
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`, so `0` is now treated as invalid and coerced to `fallbackMs`. `0` is a legitimate delay for `setTimeout`, so previously `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` meant "SIGTERM then SIGKILL immediately" and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` meant "give up immediately". Both consumers (@src/shared/runner-process.ts:3-6 and :7-10) now return the defaults (5000/2000) for that input, silently lengthening the grace/escalation window on the live spawn path (@:124 and @:119-123) for any user who had configured 0.

findings.title: Honor explicit 0 in readRunnerDurationMs instead of overriding
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code accepted parsed >= 0, so NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 (and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0) produced 0ms. The new `parsed > 0` check rejects 0 and returns fallbackMs, so those env values now silently become 5000 (line 3-6) and 2000 (line 7-10). Concretely, the grace timer at line 124 waits 5000ms instead of 0ms before SIGKILL, and the give-up timer at line 123 waits 2000ms instead of resolving immediately — an operator-set 0 is indistinguishable from unset, changing kill/cleanup timing on a live runner path.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so every changed file is deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The tail-coverage hotspot that guaranteed every changed file was assigned to some reviewed surface was deleted. `hotspots` is now `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` and is iterated directly, so any changed file the map pass did not place in one of the up-to-6 highest-risk hotspots is never passed to a deep review, producing no finding and no residual/signal. This silently drops review coverage for large PRs instead of never skipping a changed file as the removed code explicitly promised.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks instead of hardcoding empty
findings.whyItBreaks: The deep pass's `residual_risks` are no longer collected (`residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` was removed) and `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is hardcoded to `[]`. Those residuals previously reached the critic via `{{FINDINGS}}` (JSON.stringify(candidateMerged)), so a `blocks:true` residual reported by a deep hotspot could still block the final verdict. Now the signal is discarded before the critic and before `ReviewResult.residualRisks`, so `deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks)` at src/core/review.ts:122 can return PASS for a review whose deep pass reported a blocking residual.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so no changed file is silently skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the 'tail-coverage' backstop that pushed every changed file not present in the selected hotspots into an extra low-risk hotspot. After `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (:93, MAX_HOTSPOTS = 6 @:26), any hotspot dropped by the slice — and any changed file the map pass never assigned to a surface — is now never deep-reviewed. It yields no finding, no `checked` entry, and no residual risk, so `review()` can report PASS for a PR whose changed files were never inspected; the removed comment explicitly promised 'never silently skip a changed file'.

findings.title: Stop discarding deep-pass residual risks in reviewLarge
findings.whyItBreaks: `residual_risks: []` is now hardcoded on the merged candidate, and the `residuals` accumulator plus `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` were removed from the per-hotspot loop (:97-106). Previously each successful deep pass's `residual_risks` (including `blocks: true` entries) flowed into the critic prompt via `candidateMerged` at :116; now the critic always receives an empty list. A deep pass that flags a blocking unresolved risk can therefore be silently dropped and `reviewLarge` can return a PASS verdict.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage hotspot before the deep-review loop
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge caps surfaces at MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 (`slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)`, src/core/review.ts:26 and :93) and iterates only those hotspots (src/core/review.ts:97). The deleted block (old src/core/review.ts:96-110) computed `covered`/`uncovered` and pushed a tail hotspot holding every changed file absent from the selected hotspots, with the explicit promise 'never silently skip a changed file'. With that backstop gone, any changed file the map pass did not assign to one of the ≤6 selected hotspots is never passed to deep.md and can never produce a finding — silently. This triggers whenever mapResult yields >6 hotspots (the rest, and their files, are dropped) or whenever the map simply omits a changed file.

findings.title: Propagate deep-pass residual risks instead of resetting to []
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the deep loop accumulated `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` (old src/core/review.ts:115/127) and handed them to the critic via `candidateMerged.residual_risks` (old :140). Now `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is hard-coded to `[]` (src/core/review.ts:113), and the final result returns `pruned.residual_risks` (:128). The critic prompt only receives `{{FINDINGS}}` (candidateMerged JSON) + `{{PATCH}}` (patchStat), so any residual risk a deep reviewer reported — including entries with `blocks: true` — is discarded before the critic runs and can never reach `deriveVerdict` (:122). A deep pass that flags a blocking, unresolved risk can therefore be converted into a PASS for the large path (TRIGGER D: signal discarded/downgraded to the empty default).

findings.title: Restore focus/deep forwarding in large-review path
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge no longer copies bundle.focus/bundle.deep into mapBundle and no longer substitutes {{FOCUS}} in the deep prompt chain (removed .replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")). For any PR large enough to take the map->deep route the user's focus/deep options are silently dropped, while reviewSmall at src/core/review.ts:52-55 still serializes the entire bundle (including focus/deep). The same input therefore works for small PRs and is ignored for large PRs — a silent, size-dependent loss of user-provided guidance, not a compile/typing change (Bundle still declares the fields; only review.ts changed).

findings.title: formatDuration can emit '1m 60s' instead of '2m 0s'
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from the raw ms (line 90) while seconds are rounded from the remainder (line 91). When the remainder rounds up to 60, minutes and seconds are computed independently and never re-normalized, so the string is wrong. Example: ms=119500 → minutes=1, seconds=round(59500/1000)=60 → '1m 60s' (correct: '2m 0s'). Also ms=59999 → minutes=0, seconds=round(59.999)=60 → '60s' (previously '1m 0s'). The old code rounded totalSeconds first, so the carry propagated into minutes. This output is user-visible: it is rendered into the report stats/total lines via the two call sites at src/shared/render.ts:75 and src/shared/render.ts:80.

findings.title: Fix minute boundary: formatDuration can emit "1m 60s"/"60s"
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is floored from ms/60000 while seconds is independently rounded from the remainder, so a remainder of >=59500ms rounds to 60. For ms=119500 the new code yields minutes=1, seconds=Math.round(59500/1000)=60 → "1m 60s"; for ms=59999 it yields minutes=0, seconds=60 → "60s". The base version rounded to totalSeconds first (Math.round(119500/1000)=120 → "2m 0s"), so this change regresses correct output into an invalid duration. The value is user-visible in the rendered stats line (src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80).

findings.title: formatDuration emits '60s' / '1m 60s' instead of rolling seconds over
findings.whyItBreaks: Seconds are rounded from the leftover remainder (Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000)), which reaches 60 whenever ms % 60000 >= 59500. The base code computed totalSeconds first, then derived minutes=Math.floor(totalSeconds/60) and seconds=totalSeconds%60, so seconds was always < 60. The new code loses that invariant: ms=59999 renders '60s' (e.g. the per-call label at src/shared/render.ts:75 and the total at src/shared/render.ts:80) and ms=119500 renders '1m 60s' instead of '2m 0s'.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, breaking its contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function is named parsePositiveInteger and its unchanged error text says the value "requires a positive integer", but the guard was loosened to `parsed < 0`, so 0 is returned instead of rejected. Because `Number("")`, `Number(" ")` and `Number("\t")` all coerce to 0, empty/whitespace input — previously rejected — is now silently accepted as a valid value. The body no longer implements the behavior the carrier (name + message) promises, and since this is an exported public function the promise is the contract; callers validating numeric config (e.g. timeoutMs/attempts) will receive 0 rather than an error.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, contradicting its contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was loosened from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `parsePositiveInteger("0", ...)` no longer throws and returns 0. The function name and the unchanged thrown message ("requires a positive integer") still promise a strictly positive value, so this exported parser now hands callers a zero where they are documented to receive >=1. Any caller sizing attempts/timeouts/counts from this value gets a non-positive number instead of the validation error it previously relied on.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 despite promising positivity
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns 0 instead of throwing. The exported symbol name (`parsePositiveInteger`) and its only error text (`${label} requires a positive integer` @line 33) both promise that the input is validated to be strictly positive; 0 is not positive. Any caller that trusts the documented guarantee (e.g. using the result as a count/concurrency/attempts/timeout that must be >= 1) now silently gets 0 and proceeds, and the "requires a positive integer" error can no longer be produced for the 0 case. This is a contract-drift defect on an exported carrier: the promised validation is no longer implemented by the body.
